chapters.title: Chapter 4: Related Parties and Capital Allocation

lessons.title: Case Study: Value Destruction Through Group Company Lending

body.text: The cleanest way to move money out of a listed company is not theft. It is a loan, because a loan stays an asset on the balance sheet until someone admits it will never come back.

children.text: In Lesson 12 you learned to read the related party note. This case study focuses on the most damaging line in it: money lent, deposited, or advanced to entities the promoter controls. Overpriced purchases show up in margins. Excess pay shows up in costs. A loan shows up nowhere in the profit and loss account. It sits quietly among assets, often earning interest that is booked as income but never received in cash, until the day it has to be written off.
Why Lending Is the Preferred Channel

body.caption: What makes related party lending attractive to a promoter under pressure

cells: No profit impact
Cash leaves, but the balance sheet simply swaps cash for a receivable
Profit looks unchanged while asset quality quietly deteriorates
It can boost profit
Interest is accrued as income even when no cash is received
Reported earnings rise on money that may never arrive
It looks temporary
Described as short-term deposits, advances, or treasury operations
Rollovers can continue for years before anyone forces recognition
It can be disguised
Routed through subsidiaries, layered across entities, or mixed into a lender's normal loan book
Very hard to spot without reading the notes and CARO carefully

body.text: Interest accrued but not received is the tell. If a company reports growing interest income from related parties while operating cash flow lags profit year after year, the profit is being manufactured by the same loans that are draining the cash.

children.text: Coffee Day Enterprises ran Cafe Coffee Day, one of India's best known retail chains, along with coffee estates, logistics, and technology parks. Its founder, V.G. Siddhartha, was also a significant investor in other businesses and carried personal and group borrowings, much of it secured against shares.

body.title: Coffee Day: how the lending came to light

events.title: A large asset sale to reduce debt
events.description: Siddhartha sells his roughly 20% stake in IT services company Mindtree to Larsen & Toubro for about ₹3,269 crore, with the stated aim of cutting group debt.

events.title: Founder's death and a letter
events.description: Siddhartha dies, and a letter attributed to him describes intense financial pressure. The share price collapses and the board begins reviewing group transactions.

events.title: Investigation reports ₹3,535 crore moved to a promoter entity
events.description: An investigation commissioned by the company, led by a former senior CBI officer, reports that about ₹3,535 crore had been moved from seven Coffee Day subsidiaries to Mysore Amalgamated Coffee Estates Ltd, an entity linked to the founder's family.

events.title: Recovery efforts and asset sales
events.description: The company pursues recovery of the amount, sells assets to repay lenders, and faces continuing legal proceedings. Minority shareholders are left with a much smaller company.

children.text: Note where the money moved from. Not the listed parent directly, but seven subsidiaries. A shareholder reading only the standalone accounts of the listed company would have seen far less than one reading the consolidated statements, the related party note, and Form AOC-1.
Case 2: DHFL, Where Lending Was the Business

Dewan Housing Finance Corporation (DHFL) was one of India's largest housing finance companies, promoted by the Wadhawan family. For a lender, related party lending is far harder for an outsider to detect, because loans to connected entities can sit among hundreds of thousands of genuine loans and look exactly like business as usual.

body.title: DHFL: from NBFC favourite to insolvency

events.title: The NBFC funding shock
events.description: After the IL&FS defaults, a mutual fund sells DHFL bonds at a sharp discount in the secondary market. The stock falls more than 40% in a single session as investors question the company's access to funding.

events.title: Allegations of diversion
events.description: A media investigation alleges that roughly ₹31,000 crore was routed to entities linked to the promoters through shell companies. DHFL denies the allegations.

events.title: Default and downgrades
events.description: DHFL misses interest payments and rating agencies downgrade its instruments to default, freezing its access to funding.

events.title: Forensic audit and RBI action
events.description: A forensic audit commissioned by lenders reports transactions with entities linked to the promoters. In November 2019, RBI supersedes the board, and DHFL becomes the first financial services firm referred to insolvency under the special route for such companies.

events.title: Resolution and criminal proceedings
events.description: Piramal Capital's resolution plan is approved and the company changes hands. Investigating agencies register cases alleging bank fraud running into tens of thousands of crores. Equity shareholders of DHFL are left with nothing.

body.text: For lenders, the standard checks are different. Watch the mix between retail and wholesale or project loans, concentration in loans to real estate developers, the share of loans rolled over or restructured, and any gap between reported interest income and interest actually collected in cash. A lender whose wholesale book grows much faster than its retail book deserves questions.

cells: Core business
Cafe chain, coffee estates, technology parks
Housing finance
Where money went
About ₹3,535 crore from seven subsidiaries to a promoter family entity, per the company-commissioned investigation
Alleged routing to entities linked to promoters, denied by the company and subject to legal proceedings
Disguise
Inter-company transfers inside a complex group

Group funding needs during an NBFC liquidity squeeze

children.text: What the Numbers Look Like Before the Collapse

Here is an illustrative company that lends to promoter entities and accrues interest on those loans. Reported profit rises steadily. Strip out the interest accrued from related parties, none of it received in cash, and the growth disappears.

body.title: Reported profit vs profit excluding accrued related party interest (₹ crore)

series.label: Profit excluding accrued related party interest

children.text: Reported profit grew 18.4% over two years. Adjusted profit fell 3.1%. The gap is accrued interest on loans to the promoter's own companies, income the company records but never banks. If those loans eventually have to be provided for, the accrued interest is reversed too, so the earlier profits were not merely cash-free, they were temporary.

body.title: Size the Hole
body.prompt: A listed company has net worth of ₹6,000 crore. Its related party note shows ₹2,400 crore of loans and deposits outstanding with promoter group entities. If all of it had to be provided for, by what percentage would net worth fall?
body.explanation: ₹2,400 crore ÷ ₹6,000 crore = 40%. Before valuing this company on book value or price to book, ask whether you are paying for ₹6,000 crore of net worth or ₹3,600 crore. The market usually settles that question suddenly, not gradually.

children.text: The Signals, and Where They Live

body.caption: Seven checks for related party lending

cells: Loans, deposits, or advances to promoter entities, and their trend
Related party note in the annual report; half-yearly RPT filings on BSE and NSE
Loans with no repayment terms, repayable on demand, or overdue
CARO clause 3(iii), which asks the auditor about exactly this
Interest accrued but not received
Notes on other income and on loans, compared with cash flow from operations
Cash leaving through subsidiaries rather than the parent
Consolidated cash flow statement and Form AOC-1
Guarantees for group company borrowings
Contingent liabilities note
Auditor attention on recoverability
Key Audit Matters, Emphasis of Matter, or a qualified opinion
Promoter under financial pressure
Pledged percentage on screener.in and encumbrance filings, plus group company debt in the news

children.text: The last row ties this chapter back to Chapter 2. Related party lending almost never starts because a promoter is greedy in the abstract. It starts because the promoter needs money somewhere else, usually in an unlisted business, and the listed company is the most accessible source of cash. High pledging and heavy group debt are the motive. The related party note is where you see the act.

body.title: Which Disclosure Worries You Most?
body.question: You are reading the annual report of a profitable mid cap company. Which single disclosure most strongly suggests value is leaking through group lending?
options: A ₹300 crore loan to a wholly owned subsidiary that runs a manufacturing plant, of which ₹50 crore was repaid during the year
CARO clause 3(iii) stating that loans of ₹450 crore to promoter group entities have no stipulated repayment schedule and are repayable on demand, with no interest received during the year
A ₹120 crore corporate guarantee for a wholly owned subsidiary's working capital facility
Fixed deposits of ₹800 crore with scheduled commercial banks, earning market rates
body.explanation: Loans to entities outside the listed group, with no repayment schedule and no interest actually collected, are the exact profile of money that does not come back. Loans and guarantees to wholly owned subsidiaries stay inside the consolidated numbers you own, and bank deposits are genuinely liquid.

body.title: The Treasury That Is Not a Treasury
body.scenario: A mid cap NBFC listed on NSE reports steady 20% profit growth and a gross NPA ratio of just 1.2%. Reading the annual report, you find: wholesale loans to real estate developers have grown from 18% to 41% of the loan book in three years; the related party note shows ₹900 crore of loans to entities described as 'others in which directors are interested'; interest income includes ₹145 crore accrued on those loans while operating cash flow has been negative for two years; the promoter pledge has risen from 8% to 52%; and the auditor has added a Key Audit Matter on 'recoverability of certain wholesale advances'. Net worth is ₹4,200 crore.
body.prompt: How do you interpret the 1.2% gross NPA figure, and what would you do?
body.modelAnswer: Treat the 1.2% gross NPA as unreliable rather than reassuring. A loan that is rolled over or has no repayment schedule never becomes overdue, so it never shows up as an NPA. That is precisely how connected and evergreened wholesale loans stay invisible in asset quality ratios. Everything else points the same way: wholesale exposure to developers has more than doubled as a share of the book, ₹900 crore sits with entities connected to directors, ₹145 crore of income on those loans is accrued but not collected, and operating cash flow has been negative while profit grew 20%. The promoter pledge rising from 8% to 52% supplies the motive. The auditor's Key Audit Matter says a professional is already worried. The ₹900 crore alone is about 21% of net worth, and that is only the disclosed related party portion, before any losses on other developer loans. The reasonable response is to exit rather than to model a haircut, because in lenders the gap between reported and real asset quality usually closes in one step, not gradually.

body.title: Screen Your Portfolio for Group Lending Risk
steps: In the latest annual report, use the related party note to list every loan, deposit, advance, or investment to entities that are not wholly owned subsidiaries
Add them up and divide by net worth to get your worst-case provision impact
Read CARO clause 3(iii) for whether those loans have repayment terms, are overdue, or are repayable on demand
Check whether interest on those loans was actually received in cash, and compare five years of operating cash flow with net profit
In the consolidated statements and Form AOC-1, check whether cash is leaving through subsidiaries rather than the parent
Note the promoter's pledged percentage and any group company debt reported in the news
If the exposure exceeds 15% to 20% of net worth and the promoter is under pressure, treat the reported book value as unreliable

body.text: This case study describes allegations, investigation findings, regulatory actions, and court proceedings as publicly reported. Several matters remain before courts and investigating agencies, and nothing here should be read as a finding of guilt against any person or entity. It is for education only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Loans to promoter entities are the most effective leakage channel because they leave profit untouched and can even inflate it through accrued interest
A company-commissioned investigation reported about ₹3,535 crore moved from seven Coffee Day subsidiaries to a promoter family entity, which is why consolidated statements and Form AOC-1 matter
DHFL shows the hardest version: in a lender, connected loans hide inside an ordinary loan book, and equity shareholders were left with nothing after insolvency
Strip accrued related party interest out of profit; in the illustration, reported growth of 18.4% became a decline of 3.1%
Size the risk by dividing related party loans by net worth: ₹2,400 crore against ₹6,000 crore means 40% of book value depends on the promoter repaying
For lenders, low reported NPAs mean little when loans are rolled over; check the wholesale versus retail mix and interest actually collected in cash
